results.markdown:
Title: Billboard vs. TV Advertising: Cost & Effectiveness (2026)

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/billboard-vs-tv-advertising-comparison

Published Time: 2026-03-17T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Billboards and TV commercials are both "big" advertising formats. They reach a lot of people, they build brand awareness, and they've been around for decades. But for a local business deciding where to put its marketing budget, the differences between these two channels matter a lot more than the similarities.

This guide compares billboard and TV advertising across cost, targeting, creative flexibility, measurability, and real-world effectiveness for small and local businesses.

## How billboard advertising works

![Image 1: Billboard vs TV Advertising Comparison - Body1](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/7BcjkJgcMksVjgBeRq4tkA/8e93af153136389ac5a8c7d4866d24cd/body1.png)
Billboard advertising puts your message on a large physical sign in a high-traffic location. There are two main types:

**Static billboards.** A single printed advertisement displayed for a contracted period (usually 4 weeks). One advertiser owns the entire board for that period.

**Digital billboards.** An electronic display that rotates between multiple advertisers. Your ad shows for 6 to 8 seconds per rotation, typically sharing the board with 6 to 8 other advertisers. You get a fraction of the total display time.

Billboard contracts typically run on 4-week cycles, and most require a minimum commitment of 4 to 12 weeks.

## How TV advertising works today

For local businesses, [CTV (connected TV) advertising](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-connected-tv-advertising) is the relevant form of TV advertising. Traditional broadcast and cable TV are generally too expensive and too broad for most local businesses.

CTV runs your 30-second commercial on streaming platforms like Hulu, Peacock, Tubi, and 100+ other channels. With platforms like [Adwave](https://adwave.com/how-it-works), you can target specific demographics and geographic areas, get real-time analytics, and launch campaigns starting at $30 a day.

## Cost comparison

![Image 2: Billboard vs TV Advertising Comparison - Body2](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/5ZftZ0DUcnnIwCks09aOem/8a1ecd30655b5bf990cf18d73b028f04/body2.png)
### Billboard costs

Billboard pricing varies dramatically by market and location:

**Static billboards:**

*   Small market: $750 to $2,000/month

*   Medium market: $2,000 to $5,000/month

*   Large market: $5,000 to $15,000+/month

*   Premium locations (highway interchanges, city centers): $10,000 to $30,000+/month

**Digital billboards:**

*   Typically 30 to 50% less than static because you share the board

*   Small market: $500 to $1,500/month

*   Medium market: $1,500 to $4,000/month

**Additional costs:**

*   Design: $200 to $1,000 for professional billboard creative

*   Production and installation (static): $300 to $1,000

*   No targeting beyond location selection

### CTV costs

**Campaign costs:**

*   CPMs range from [$15 to $35](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-cpm-by-platform) (cost per 1,000 impressions)

*   Adwave campaigns start at $30 a day

*   Most local businesses invest $500 to $2,500/month

*   Ad creation is free with Adwave (AI generates a 30-second commercial in about 2 minutes)

*   No production crew, studio rental, or media buyer required

## Targeting and reach

### Billboard targeting

Billboard "targeting" is purely location-based. You pick a board, and whoever drives or walks past it sees your ad. That's both its strength and its limitation.

**What you can control:**

*   Physical location of the board

*   Multiple boards in different locations (at additional cost)

**What you can't control:**

*   Who sees it (everyone passing by, regardless of whether they're in your target market)

*   When they see it (24/7, no dayparting)

*   How often the same person sees it (depends on their commute patterns)

*   Whether they look at it (many drivers don't notice billboards)

The Out of Home Advertising Association of America estimates that a well-placed billboard in a medium market generates 30,000 to 50,000 daily impressions. But "impressions" for billboards means vehicles passing by, not people reading and processing your message.

### CTV targeting

CTV targeting is precise and multi-dimensional:

**What you can control:**

*   [Geographic targeting](https://adwave.com/resources/geofencing-marketing-local-business) down to zip codes and DMAs

*   Demographics (age, gender, household income)

*   Interests and viewing behaviors

*   Frequency (how many times each household sees your ad)

*   Flight dates (when your campaign runs)

**What this means in practice:** A local restaurant can target households within 10 miles, with household income above $75K, aged 30 to 55. A billboard near the restaurant reaches everyone driving by, including tourists passing through, teenagers without spending power, and people who live 50 miles away.

## Creative impact

![Image 3: Billboard vs TV Advertising Comparison - Body3](https://media.adwave.com/fia320z3blxi/7KmqPuWEHYIUEHpzW7ZePJ/b13461ca9165c1c38a87f9b4b98570ed/body3.png)
### Billboard creative limitations

Billboards impose severe creative constraints:

*   **5 to 7 words maximum.** Drivers have 5 to 7 seconds to read your billboard at highway speed. Any more text and they won't process it.

*   **Single static image.** You get one visual frame to communicate everything. No motion, no sound, no story.

*   **No sound.** A billboard is a silent medium. You can't demonstrate your product, share a testimonial, or use music to create an emotional connection.

*   **No interaction.** Viewers can't click, call, or respond in the moment (though some add phone numbers or URLs that few people remember).

*   **Weather and visibility.** Rain, fog, darkness, and sun glare all reduce billboard visibility. Digital boards handle darkness better, but other conditions still apply.

### CTV creative advantages

A 30-second CTV commercial has dramatically more creative power:

*   **Sight, sound, and motion.** Show your restaurant's food being prepared, your dental office's friendly team, your auto shop's clean facility. Video communicates things that a static image and 7 words never could.

*   **Storytelling.** Thirty seconds is enough time to present a problem, introduce your solution, and include a call to action. You can tell a complete story.

*   **Emotional connection.** Music, voice-over, and visual storytelling create emotional responses that drive brand preference. Research from the Video Advertising Bureau shows that video advertising creates significantly stronger emotional engagement than static formats.

*   **Full viewer attention.** CTV ads are non-skippable on most platforms, with completion rates above 90%. Compare that to a billboard that might get a 2-second glance from a distracted driver.

## Measurability

### Billboard measurement

Billboard measurement is notoriously imprecise:

*   **Traffic counts.** The primary metric is vehicles passing by per day, provided by the billboard company. This tells you potential exposure, not actual attention.

*   **No engagement data.** You don't know if anyone read your billboard, remembered it, or acted on it.

*   **Attribution is nearly impossible.** There's no reliable way to connect a billboard to a specific customer, purchase, or phone call unless you use a unique promo code or vanity URL (which most viewers won't remember).

*   **Industry metric: DEC.** Daily Effective Circulation estimates how many people might see your billboard each day. It's based on traffic data, not actual viewing behavior.

### CTV measurement

CTV provides significantly more data:

*   **Impression counts.** Exact number of times your ad was served to households.

*   **Reach and frequency.** How many unique households saw your ad, and how many times each.

*   **Completion rates.** What percentage of viewers watched the full 30-second ad (typically 90%+).

*   **[Branded search lift](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-attribution-small-business).** Measurable increases in people searching for your business name after seeing your ad.

*   **Website traffic correlation.** Increases in direct and organic traffic during campaign periods.

*   **Real-time dashboards.** Platforms like Adwave provide real-time analytics so you can see performance as your campaign runs.

## When billboards make sense

Billboards aren't always the wrong choice. They can work well in specific situations:

**Directional signage.** If your business is near a highway exit, a billboard directing traffic to your location ("Exit 42, turn right") can be effective because the viewer can act immediately.

**Brand reinforcement in high-traffic corridors.** If you're already running other advertising and want to add a visual presence along a specific route your customers drive d

results.title: How much does DOOH advertising cost? | AdQuick
results.markdown:
Title: How much does DOOH advertising cost? | AdQuick

URL Source: https://www.adquick.com/answers/dooh-campaigns/how-much-does-dooh-digital-out-of-home-advertising-cost

Markdown Content:
## Short answer

DOOH advertising CPMs typically range from $3 to $20, though premium placements like Times Square or major airports can exceed $50. Monthly digital billboard costs run from $1,200 in smaller markets to $15,000 or more in major cities. Programmatic campaigns generally require a minimum spend of $10,000 to $50,000.

## What campaigns actually cost on AdQuick

Campaigns built on multi-format ran a median $39,300 in total campaign spend, with a typical range of $14,200 to $68,450 (80 campaigns). Campaign composition varies widely, so treat the midpoint as indicative rather than a quote.

_Source: AdQuick marketplace transactions, July 2025 to June 2026. Figures are transacted prices, not rate cards; percentiles are shown as typical range (25th to 75th) around the median._

## How DOOH advertising is priced

DOOH costs are expressed in two main ways: Cost Per Mille (CPM), the cost per 1,000 impressions, and flat or monthly rates, fixed fees per screen or location used most often for premium direct buys.

The CPM model makes it easier to compare cost efficiency across formats and venues. Flat-rate pricing suits high-impact placements where impression volumes are large and a fixed cost simplifies budgeting.

Typical CPM ranges by format:

*   Programmatic DOOH: $3 to $20, depending on inventory quality and location
*   Digital billboards: $5 to $10
*   Smaller screens in high-traffic but non-premium locations such as subways or gas stations: $2 to $6
*   Premium urban placements at major airports or iconic intersections: $50 or more

## What drives the cost of a DOOH campaign

Several variables push costs up or down.

**Location** is the single largest factor. Premium urban centers with heavy foot traffic or tourist presence command the highest rates because of guaranteed high impressions and brand prestige. Rural and suburban placements offer lower costs but reduced reach.

**Screen size and format** matter significantly. Large-format digital billboards cost more due to their visibility. Indoor screens in malls typically run $750 to $2,500 per month, while digital supermarket screens run roughly $800 to $1,500 per month. Specialized formats such as digital kiosks tend to be less expensive but reach niche audiences.

**Buying method** shapes both cost and flexibility. Programmatic DOOH offers shorter commitments and sometimes lower entry points, though auction dynamics create variable CPMs. Direct buys involve fixed pricing with guaranteed inventory but less flexibility.

**Audience targeting and data integration** add cost. Layering in geo-fencing, first-party data, or real-time triggers improves campaign efficiency but commands a premium on most programmatic platforms.

**Campaign duration and frequency** affect unit cost. Longer campaigns and higher-frequency buys generally reduce CPMs or unlock volume discounts, though they require larger upfront commitments.

## Monthly and campaign budget benchmarks

Monthly spend by market size:

| Placement type | Typical monthly cost |
| --- | --- |
| Digital billboard, small market | From $1,200 |
| Digital billboard, major city | $15,000 or more |
| Digital mall screens | $750 to $2,500 |
| Digital supermarket screens | $800 to $1,500 |
| Large premium screens (Times Square, airports) | Thousands to tens of thousands per screen |

Campaign minimums vary by buying approach. Programmatic platforms typically require $10,000 to $50,000 per campaign to access meaningful inventory and targeting options. Local or regional campaigns negotiated directly can start below $10,000, and some small business campaigns begin as low as $1,000 to $5,000 per month depending on location and network. National multi-city campaigns generally require $50,000 or more to achieve meaningful scale and frequency.

A straightforward way to estimate reach: divide your total budget by the CPM. A $10,000 budget at a $5 CPM yields approximately 2 million impressions.

## Trends shaping DOOH costs

Programmatic adoption continues to accelerate. Programmatic DOOH spending is projected to grow from $6.83 billion to $12.88 billion by 2030, which is broadening access to premium inventory and enabling better targeting and measurement for advertisers who previously lacked the budgets for direct buys.

Auction-based pricing is replacing some fixed-rate negotiations. For buyers, this can lower CPMs on certain inventory but introduces more variability in what a given placement will cost from one campaign to the next.

Cross-channel integrations, particularly DOOH-to-mobile retargeting, are increasing campaign effectiveness but also adding incremental costs for data and technology. Improved attribution partnerships are helping advertisers calculate ROI more precisely, though they typically require higher platform investment.

Creative complexity is an underappreciated cost driver. Managing dynamic content across multiple screen formats increases production costs beyond the media spend itself, a consideration worth building into any DOOH budget.

## How AdQuick handles billboard costs

AdQuick's marketplace lets buyers compare [billboard costs](https://www.adquick.com/billboard-cost) across digital and traditional formats in one place, covering local direct-buy inventory alongside programmatic options. Planners can filter by location, format, and audience data to model CPMs and monthly spend before committing, which helps both small regional campaigns and larger national buys stay within budget. Measurement tools built into the platform connect impressions to downstream outcomes, making it easier to evaluate whether a given placement delivered the reach and efficiency the budget required.

results.title: Programmatic DOOH Trends in 2026: How Self-Serve is Lowering Barriers for Local Brands
results.markdown:
Title: Programmatic DOOH Trends in 2026: How Self-Serve is Lowering Barriers for Local Brands

URL Source: https://take10media.com/blog/self-serve-dooh-trends-2026-local-brands/

Published Time: 2026-06-16T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
## At a Glance

For decades, digital out-of-home (DOOH) advertising was a premium marketing channel reserved exclusively for enterprise brands with massive budgets. The traditional process of buying outdoor media was slow, manual, and required heavy upfront financial commitments. However, the landscape has fundamentally shifted. In 2026, **programmatic DOOH and self-serve ad networks** are democratizing the industry, lowering entry barriers, and allowing local businesses to launch high-impact screen campaigns with micro-budgets. In this article, we explore the major DOOH trends of 2026 and examine how retail-based touchpoints like convenience store and ATM screens are outperforming traditional highway billboards for local brands.

* * *

## The Democratization of Outdoor Advertising: From $25k to Micro-Budgets

Historically, entering the outdoor advertising space was a daunting task for small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs). If a local restaurant, real estate agent, or boutique service provider wanted to advertise on a digital highway billboard, they were met with rigid agency contracts, high production fees, and steep minimum spend requirements. It was not uncommon for traditional outdoor media campaigns to demand a minimum commitment of $25,000 or more.

In 2026, programmatic technology has shattered these barriers. According to a comprehensive industry analysis on [programmatic DOOH for small business outdoor advertising in 2026](https://emarketed.com/digital-marketing/programmatic-dooh-small-business-outdoor-advertising-2026/), the minimum entry threshold has plummeted from those traditional five-figure sums to highly accessible monthly budgets on programmatic platforms. This shift is driven by automated bidding, real-time inventory allocation, and self-serve ad portals that bypass traditional media brokers entirely.

By allowing advertisers to purchase ad space on a “per-play” or “per-impression” basis, programmatic DOOH enables local brands to compete side-by-side with national corporations. You no longer need a dedicated media-buying team or thousands of dollars in liquid cash to get your brand on a premium digital screen. Instead, you can allocate a modest daily budget, monitor performance, and scale your campaign as your business grows.

* * *

## Visualizing the Shift: How Programmatic DOOH Lowers Barriers

To understand how modern ad tech has transformed the advertising landscape, we can look at the core barriers that previously kept local brands out of the market and how programmatic systems have resolved them.

![Image 1: Infographic showing how programmatic DOOH lowers barriers for SMBs in 2026](https://take10media.com/_astro/infographic-self-serve-dooh-barriers.CK0HEXEX_Spb1l.jpeg)

How programmatic DOOH and self-serve technology have systematically dismantled the traditional barriers to entry for local businesses.

As illustrated above, the transition from manual, broker-led buying to automated, self-serve platforms has unlocked unprecedented flexibility, transparency, and affordability for local businesses.

* * *

## Highway Billboards vs. Retail Touchpoints: Where Local Brands Win

While digital billboards along major highways are highly visible, they are rarely the most effective choice for local, neighborhood-focused brands. Highway advertising is designed for broad, top-of-funnel brand awareness. It targets fast-moving drivers who have extremely short dwell times (often only 3 to 5 seconds) and are focused on navigating traffic rather than absorbing marketing messages. Furthermore, highway billboards are expensive and lack geographic precision—you are paying to reach commuters who may live miles away from your physical business.

This is where the [Take 10 Media self-serve ad network](https://take10media.com/self-serve/) offers a superior alternative. Instead of placing ads on distant highway billboards, Take 10 Media positions high-definition digital screens directly inside local convenience stores and on ATM terminals.

These retail-based DOOH touchpoints offer several distinct advantages for local advertisers:

1.   **Captive Audiences and High Dwell Time:** When a customer is standing in line at a convenience store checkout counter or waiting for cash to dispense at an ATM, their dwell time increases dramatically. Instead of a fleeting 3-second glance, your video ad captures their attention for 1 to 3 minutes in a distraction-free environment.
2.   **Point-of-Decision Marketing:** Retail screens are positioned at the absolute point of decision—where consumers are holding their wallets, ready to make a purchase. This proximity makes it incredibly easy to trigger impulse buys or direct immediate foot traffic to a nearby business.
3.   **Hyper-Local Relevance:** Convenience stores and ATMs serve as hyper-local community hubs. By targeting screens in specific ZIP codes or individual store locations, local service providers and retail brands can ensure that 100% of their ad spend is directed at active, local residents who live and shop in their immediate trade area.

For a deeper dive into selecting the absolute best physical locations for your campaigns, read our guide on [where to launch self-serve video ad campaigns](https://take10media.com/blog/where-to-launch-self-serve-video-ad-campaigns/).

* * *

## Comparing Traditional DOOH vs. Programmatic Self-Serve Networks

To fully appreciate the value of modern programmatic networks, let us compare the characteristics of traditional, managed outdoor advertising campaigns against modern self-serve DOOH networks:

| Feature | Traditional Managed DOOH | Programmatic Self-Serve DOOH (Take 10 Media) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Minimum Budget** | High minimums (often $10,000 to $25,000+) | Flexible, accessible micro-budgets (no high minimums) |
| **Contract Commitments** | Rigid, long-term contracts (weeks or months) | Pay-as-you-go, pause or adjust anytime |
| **Buying Process** | Manual negotiations, brokers, RFPs, and emails | Instant digital buying via a 24/7 [Ad Portal](https://cms.take10media.com/ads) |
| **Creative Approvals** | Slow, manual reviews taking several days | Automated or rapid digital review (under 24-48 hours) |
| **Targeting Precision** | Broad, regional bundles with low granularity | Screen-by-screen, ZIP code, or neighborhood selection |
| **Performance Analytics** | Delayed post-campaign PDF reports with estimates | Real-time, transparent proof-of-play dashboard |
| **Creative Flexibility** | Static images or highly restricted video changes | Dynamic video creatives, instant updates, A/B testing |

This comparison highlights why local businesses are rapidly shifting their marketing dollars away from traditional offline media and toward self-serve retail networks. To learn more about how this self-directed method compares with traditional managed agency services, check out our comparative analysis of [self-serve advertising vs. managed campaigns](https://take10media.com/blog/self-serve-advertising-vs-managed-campaigns/).

* * *

## Key DOOH Trends Driving Growth in 2026

As we progress through 2026, several key trends are shaping the future of programmatic digital out-of-home advertising:

### 1. The Proliferation of Retail Media Networks (RMNs)

Retailers are realizing that their physical stores are highly valuable media assets. By installing digital screens at high-traffic checkout counters and ATM terminals, retailers are creating physical retail media networks. This allows local advertisers to reach shoppers at the exact moment they are making purchasing decisions. To understand how retail screens plug into this wider landscape, explore our analysis of the [Self-Serve Retail Media Network](https://take10media.com/blog/self-serve-retail-media-network/) trend.

### 2. Integration of Mobile and DOOH

In 2026, smart marketers are pairing their DOOH campaigns with mobile advertising. For example, a local business can run a high-impact video ad on a convenience store screen and simultaneously run localized mobile display ads targeting users within the same geofence. This multi-channel approach reinforces brand familiarity and drives higher conversion rates.

### 3. Focus on Creative Optimization

With self-serve platforms, advertisers have complete control over their creative assets. In 2026, the trend is toward short, high-energy, silent-first video creatives. Because retail environments can be busy and noisy, successful ads rely on bold typography, vibrant animations, and clear QR codes to drive engagement without relying on audio. For actionable tips on designing high-conversion creatives, read our guide on [how to buy self-serve ads](https://take10media.com/blog/buy-self-serve-ads-guide/).

results.markdown:
Title: Local TV ad cost: broadcast, cable and streaming

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/local-tv-ad-cost-2026

Final URL: https://adwave.com/resources/local-tv-ad-cost

Published Time: 2025-05-20T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Insights

## How much a local TV ad costs: broadcast, cable and streaming

Dated cost ranges for local broadcast and cable TV spots, what moves the price, and how streaming TV budgets compare.

[David Naffis](https://adwave.com/about/team/david-naffis/)May 20, 2025 Updated October 28, 2026

![Image 1: Local TV ad cost: broadcast, cable and streaming](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/7aecb255b4e511b793459e524ca735179066bd6a450e67fdf8e4ae1633462a0c.jpg)

A local TV ad cost usually runs from a few hundred dollars to several thousand per airing. Market size and daypart set most of that range, according to 2026 guidance from Comcast Advertising and National Media Spots. Production is a separate cost.

Streaming TV is usually sold per thousand impressions (CPM) instead of per spot, and campaigns can start on small daily budgets.

The figures below are the most specific dated ones available for local TV. Each row gives one figure and its unit, because per-spot, per-month and CPM prices answer different questions.

| Format | Figure | Unit | Publisher | Published |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local placements (broadcast or cable) | [A few hundred to a few thousand dollars](https://comcastadvertising.com/insights/knowledge-hub/local-tv-advertising/) | Per placement, by market and schedule | Comcast Advertising | Date not stated |
| Local broadcast spots | [A few hundred to several thousand dollars](https://nationalmediaspots.com/what-should-brands-know-about-tv-advertising-costs/) | Per spot, by market size and daypart | National Media Spots | June 13, 2026 |
| Local broadcast TV | $500 to $10,000 | Per month | National Media Spots | June 13, 2026 |
| Regional cable TV | $1,000 to $20,000 | Per month | National Media Spots | June 13, 2026 |
| Streaming/CTV | $500 to $50,000+ | Per month | National Media Spots | June 13, 2026 |
| Streaming/CTV | $15 to $40+ | CPM | National Media Spots | June 13, 2026 |
| TV, 30-second spot | $5 to $30 | CPM | Amazon Ads | Date not stated |
| Super Bowl 30-second spot (for scale) | About $8 million average, some above $10 million | Per spot, airtime only | NBC via Bloomberg, reported by [Moonb’s 2026 commercial cost guide](https://www.moonb.io/blog/how-much-is-a-30-second-commercial) | Jan 29, 2026 |

These are publisher estimates. None of the sources states a methodology or measurement period, and none of them is a station rate card. No public, dated dataset breaks local spot rates down by market size and daypart, so treat the ranges as a starting point for a conversation with a station or cable sales team. For network and national pricing next to these local numbers, see our guide to [national and local TV advertising costs](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-cost).

## How stations price a local spot

Local broadcast time is priced with two numbers: the market’s cost per point and the program’s rating. A research guide from the Lincoln Library describes the [SQAD cost-per-point method](https://guides.lndlibrary.org/c.php?g=359924&p=2432226): take the SQAD cost per point for the market and multiply it by the Nielsen rating of the program airing at that time. The result approximates the price of the spot.

![Image 2: Producer at a mixing desk in a small local TV station control room in the evening](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/d38da8d846d6dd9a4b544bf707533a2a4919a75ea84fda30ec662fb0111a3e58.jpg)

That formula explains both drivers. A higher-rated program carries more points, so the same market charges more for an ad in local news or prime time than for one at 2 AM. This is also why a spot in a top-10 market and a spot in a small DMA can differ by an order of magnitude. Our comparison of [local vs national TV buys](https://adwave.com/resources/local-vs-national-tv-advertising) covers when each scale makes sense.

Television sells a placement in a specific program, daypart and market. Streaming sells a quantity of impressions to a defined audience, often through an auction. Converting a spot price to a CPM and setting it next to a streaming CPM is common, but the impressions aren’t the same goods. A TV impression is often a shared, full-screen household view, while a streaming impression can be a connected TV or a phone.

## What moves the price: market size, daypart and season

Four factors account for most of the difference between two local quotes:

![Image 3: Family watching television together on a sofa in a lamp-lit living room in the evening](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/aaa528bf33d96425d61914c202c624e3fb602c974f4f13177646c468b931ef2f.jpg)

*   **Market size.** Smaller DMAs generally cost less and major metropolitan areas cost more, per Comcast Advertising.
*   **Daypart.** Prime time (typically 8 to 11 PM) carries the highest rates because viewing peaks then. Early morning, daytime and late night cost less, according to National Media Spots.
*   **Ad length.** Fifteen-second spots are usually priced below 30-second spots, though rates vary by network and placement.
*   **Season and congestion.** Rates rise in crowded windows such as the fourth quarter, major sports periods and local election cycles.

Off-peak and remnant inventory is the usual entry point for a small advertiser testing broadcast, but it comes with less control over exactly when the ad runs. For the longer-term direction of prices, see our analysis of [whether TV ad costs are rising](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-advertising-cost-trends).

## What changed since the last release: political money in 2026

BIA Advisory Services updated its 2026 U.S. Local Advertising Forecast on September 14, 2026, and the change is mostly political money. BIA now [projects total 2026 local ad revenue at $186.1 billion](https://www.bia.com/press-releases/bia-forecast-political-spending-lifts-2026-local-ad-market-to-186-1-billion/). According to that September release, the figure is [up $1.6 billion and about 9% above 2025](https://www.bia.com/press-releases/bia-forecast-political-spending-lifts-2026-local-ad-market-to-186-1-billion/), measured against BIA’s [April 2026 estimate of $184.5 billion](https://www.bia.com/press-releases/bia-revises-2026-local-ad-forecast-total-spend-to-reach-184-5-billion-2/).

The September update puts local political spending at $9.7 billion for 2026, up from $8.4 billion in April. Of that $1.3 billion increase, BIA says $1.2 billion went to TV OTA (broadcast) and TV OTT (streaming). Its first look at 2027 has political spending falling to about $1.1 billion in the off-cycle year, with total local revenue roughly flat at $186.5 billion. All of these are forecasts, not measured spending.

For a local business, the practical effect is inventory. Political campaigns compete for the same local broadcast time in the run-up to the midterms. That displacement hits local TV harder than streaming, so commercial advertisers can face higher rates or fewer available spots until the election passes. Campaigns weighing their own buys can read our page on [TV advertising for political campaigns](https://adwave.com/industries/political/local-campaigns/tv-advertising-political-campaigns).

## Production is a separate line

Every figure in the table above is airtime only. The commercial itself costs extra. Moonb’s 2026 guide puts a simple local spot at $1,500 to $10,000 for production. That covers a videographer or small crew, one location, one day and a straightforward edit. Professional mid-range work runs $10,000 to $50,000. On a modest local schedule, production can rival or exceed the first month of media. Our breakdown of [TV commercial production costs](https://adwave.com/resources/tv-ad-production-costs) goes through each tier.

## Streaming TV as a local alternative

Streaming TV lets a business target a DMA, ZIP code or radius and pay by CPM, with much lower minimums than a broadcast schedule. National Media Spots notes that CTV campaigns can launch on $500 to $1,000 a month. Amazon Ads describes streaming pricing as more flexible, with lower minimum spends and the ability to cap budgets.

![Image 4: Bakery owner planning advertising at a café table beside a pastry display case in morning light](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/1dd684036235bd28a24d82c3ecbfa7dda8728e484468e7c5d35a323db7d34089.jpg)

Streaming has limits. It usually guarantees impressions, not delivery within a target demographic the way large TV buys can. A small budget spread over too wide an audience may deliver too little frequency to register. ## Frequently Asked Questions About Blip Billboards

 How much does digital billboard advertising cost on Blip? 
Blip digital billboard advertising starts at $0.01 per 8-second play. There's no monthly minimum and no contract; you only pay when your ad displays. That's a sharp contrast to traditional billboard pricing, which averages $3,953 per month and ranges from $250 to $100,000+ depending on market. For a full breakdown of traditional billboard costs by market, format, and location, see our [billboard cost guide](https://www.blipbillboards.com/cost/) .

 Is there a minimum budget required for billboard advertising with Blip? 
There's no required minimum and no contract. You can start with just a few dollars per day to test a single market, then scale based on early performance.

 How much money does a 30-second ad cost? 
A 30-second ad is not sold as one block on digital billboards. Blip uses digital billboard advertising pricing based on 8-second displays.

 How does Blip pricing compare to a traditional 4-week billboard lease? 
A traditional 4-week digital billboard lease averages $3,953 per month nationally and ranges from $250 in rural markets to $100,000+ in premium urban locations.

 Are there any hidden fees beyond the per-play cost? 
No. Blip doesn't charge setup fees, platform fees, agency fees, or monthly retainers.

 Can I see billboard advertising pricing before I commit to a campaign? 
Yes, you can see pricing before you launch any campaign. Blip shows pricing for billboard advertising for each location, including estimated cost per display and traffic data.

 What affects billboard advertising cost? 
Billboard advertising cost is mainly affected by location, traffic volume, time of day, and advertiser demand. With per-play pricing, these factors help determine how much each blip costs.
